question: How often should I change my filter?
wanted: filter every one to three months

facts.text: Air filters: A furnace or central-air filter catches dust before it reaches the blower and coil. A clogged filter cuts airflow, makes the system work harder and can cause uneven rooms or a frozen coil. Many filters are changed every one to three months; a thin one in a home with pets or heavy dust may need it sooner, and a thicker one may last longer.

question: What's an ERV?

facts.text: ERV and HRV ventilators: Tight, modern homes need a way to bring in fresh air. An HRV, a heat recovery ventilator, pulls stale indoor air out and fresh outdoor air in, and passes the heat from the outgoing air to the incoming air so less heating energy is lost. An ERV, an energy recovery ventilator, does the same and also moves some moisture between the two air streams. ERVs are more common in places with humid summers, and HRVs in colder, drier places. The two airstreams never mix.

question: What's the difference between steam heat and hot water heat?

facts.text: Hot-water boilers and baseboard: Many newer buildings and houses have a hot-water boiler. It heats water and pumps it through a closed loop of pipes to radiators or to fin-tube baseboard along the walls, then the water returns to the boiler. A hot-water system usually has a pressure and temperature gauge on the boiler and an expansion tank nearby that absorbs the extra volume as the water heats.
Steam boilers and radiators: Steam heat can be uneven from room to room. Radiators near the boiler tend to heat first.
Steam boilers and radiators: Hissing from a radiator vent while it fills with steam is normal. Spitting water from a vent is not, and a technician should look at it.

keyword: Heating systems in New York City homes: Most homes in New York City are heated by a boiler or a furnace. A boiler heats water, or turns it into steam, that runs through pipes to radiators or baseboard heaters in each room. A furnace heats air and blows it through ducts and vents. Older apartment buildings usually have steam heat; houses and newer buildings more often have hot-water boilers or furnaces. Many boilers and furnaces burn natural gas or oil.

Thermostats: A thermostat in a poor spot, such as in direct sun, near a vent or on a drafty wall, reads the wrong temperature and can make the system run too long or too little. Steam and hot-water boilers usually have a thermostat on a wall and a control on the boiler itself that limits the water temperature.

question: When does the landlord have to give me heat?

facts.text: New York City heat season: In New York City, the legal heat season for apartments runs from October 1 through May 31. During those months, landlords must keep apartments at least 68 degrees between 6 AM and 10 PM when it is below 55 degrees outside, and at least 62 degrees overnight. Tenants without heat can report it to 311.
